## February 29, 1960 — A Monday That History Has Used Before

Your birthday has a history before you. February 29 does not merely appear rarely — it has appeared, over the centuries, at moments strange enough to suggest the calendar was making a point.

---

**On February 29, 1504, Christopher Columbus manipulated an eclipse to save his crew's lives.** Stranded on Jamaica, his ships rotting and unfit to sail, Columbus and his men were dependent on the local Arawak people for food. When relations soured and provisions stopped coming, Columbus consulted his almanac. He knew a total lunar eclipse was coming. He summoned the Arawak leaders, told them his god was displeased and would extinguish the moon as punishment, and watched the eclipse begin on schedule. Terrified, they promised to resume supplying the crew. Columbus "relented" as the moon returned. It is one of the most audacious deployments of scientific knowledge in recorded history, and it happened on this date, 456 years before you arrived.

**On February 29, 1792, the composer Gioachino Rossini was born.** He became the most celebrated leapling in history — famous enough in his lifetime that his unusual birthday was itself a biographical fact people remembered. Rossini made regular jokes about being a quarter of his actual age. He wrote the barber of Seville, the William Tell Overture, and dozens of operas that defined European musical culture. He died in 1868 at the biological age of 76, having celebrated the date of his birth 19 times. You are part of a small and specific tradition: people for whom the calendar withholds the birthday three years running and then returns it.

**Twenty-six days before you were born, a British Prime Minister stood in Pretoria and told South Africa that its future was already decided.** On February 3, 1960, Harold Macmillan addressed the South African parliament and delivered what became known as the Wind of Change speech. "The wind of change is blowing through this continent," he told them, "and whether we like it or not, this growth of national consciousness is a political fact." He was telling apartheid South Africa, in its own parliament, that Britain would not back it — that the age of European dominion over Africa was ending regardless of what any white minority government preferred. The South Africans were furious. The speech reverberated across the continent. You were born into a world where the most powerful remaining empire had publicly declared the age of empire over.

**Seventy-two days after your birth, the birth control pill was approved.** On May 11, 1960, the FDA approved Enovid as the first oral contraceptive. It was the culmination of decades of work by Margaret Sanger and others, and its arrival transformed the terms on which women could make decisions about their own lives. The social changes it enabled — in work, in family structure, in sexual culture, in the feminist movements of the 1960s and 70s — unfolded across the same decades you grew up through. You were born three months before one of the most consequential inventions of the twentieth century entered the world.

**The Cold War lurched toward crisis in the months after your birth.** On May 1, 1960, a CIA pilot named Francis Gary Powers was shot down over the Soviet Union in a U-2 spy plane at 70,000 feet. Eisenhower initially denied the flight was a reconnaissance mission; the Soviets produced the wreckage and the pilot. The Paris Summit between Eisenhower and Khrushchev collapsed. The brief thaw in superpower relations froze over again. You were two months old when the most dangerous bilateral relationship in human history took a sharp turn for the worse.

**The year you were born, OPEC was founded.** In September 1960, representatives of Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Venezuela met in Baghdad and formed the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries. The organization was little-noticed at first. Its significance would not be fully felt until the oil embargo of 1973, when you were thirteen — the event that ended the era of cheap energy and permanently altered the economic assumptions of the industrialized world. You were born the same year as the institution that would define one of the central crises of your adolescence.

---

**The arc of 66 years, and 16 actual birthdays.**

Most people born in 1960 have a birthday every year. You have one on the calendar every four. The years in between require a decision — February 28 or March 1, the day before or the day after, the borrowed date or the deferred one. It is a small but persistent reminder that you exist in a slightly different relationship to the calendar than almost everyone you know.

In those 66 years: the wind of change Macmillan described swept Africa and then kept going — through Eastern Europe, through the Soviet Union, through apartheid itself. The birth control pill reshaped gender relations in ways that are still working themselves out. The Cold War that produced the U-2 crisis ended without a nuclear exchange. OPEC's power rose, shaped the 1970s, and became one variable among many in an energy system now transforming under the pressure of climate.

You were born on a day Columbus once used to outwit an empire and Rossini used to laugh about in salons across Europe. The date has a personality — rare, slightly irregular, occasionally decisive. You are part of its small and particular lineage.
